events.title: Samsung Internet browser launched
events.summary: Samsung shipped its Internet browser on May 3, 2012 with the Galaxy S III — a WebKit-based mobile browser preinstalled on Samsung Android devices.
events.about: Samsung Internet became the default browser on hundreds of millions of Galaxy phones — often the first browser many Android users encounter outside Chrome. It added ad blocking, extensions, and later Chromium alignment while staying tied to Samsung's mobile ecosystem.

narrative.whyChosen: Samsung Internet is a major mobile browser by install base, not just market-share headlines.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved OEM browsers could compete with Chrome on Android through device bundling.
narrative.problemSolved: Samsung needed a controllable mobile browser integrated with Galaxy hardware and services.

events.title: Laravel 3.2 released
events.summary: Laravel migrated core request/response handling to Symfony's HttpFoundation component.
events.about: Instead of maintaining its own HTTP layer, Laravel adopted Symfony's battle-tested request/response objects. For developers: handling cookies, headers, and responses works the same way across Symfony, Laravel, and other PHP tools — less duplicated code in the PHP ecosystem.

narrative.whyChosen: This is the clearest example of Laravel embracing Symfony instead of maintaining parallel HTTP stacks.
narrative.whyImportant: Shared components meant PHP developers could move between Laravel, Symfony, and Drupal with familiar HTTP primitives.
narrative.problemSolved: Maintaining custom request/response code duplicated effort across the PHP ecosystem.

events.title: Samsung Galaxy S III released
events.summary: Samsung began selling the Samsung Galaxy S III — 4.8-inch HD Super AMOLED and Smart Stay — Samsung's breakout global Android flagship.
events.about: The Galaxy S series remained Android's volume flagship counterweight to iPhone. 4.8-inch hd super amoled and smart stay — samsung's breakout global android flagship. Developers testing Android builds routinely validated on Galaxy S hardware as the default non-Pixel reference.

narrative.whyChosen: The Samsung Galaxy S III continued Samsung's annual Android flagship cadence.
narrative.whyImportant: Galaxy S devices set the hardware bar millions of Android users and developers encounter.
narrative.problemSolved: Android needed consistent premium hardware for testing flagship features each year.
